_comment: Session checkpoint policy — guarantees a SESSION FILE ON DISK AT ALL TIMES (user requirement 2026-06-12: 'WE MUST HAVE A SESSION FILE IN DISK'). Two complementary layers: (1) the hibernate image in the swapfile carries the full RAM session, but only exists from hibernate events and is consumed on resume; (2) THIS — periodic read-only btrfs snapshots of the home subvolume. Apps persist their own session state into home continuously (browser sessionstore, editor autosaves, KDE config, tmux), so a home snapshot IS a recoverable session checkpoint that survives shutdown, crash, and firmware power-cut. CoW snapshots cost ~0 bytes until files diverge. Consumed by configuration_session-checkpoint.nix.

checkpoint._comment: btrfs_root must be the mounted pool top-level. source_subvol is snapshotted READ-ONLY into snapshot_dir/<UTC-timestamp>. Nested subvolumes (e.g. container storage inside home) are automatically excluded by btrfs — desirable, they are not session state. interval_minutes drives the systemd timer; retention_count is a simple newest-N prune (24 × 15 min = 6 h sliding window).

shutdown_checkpoint._comment: REBOOT/SHUTDOWN MUST ALWAYS SAVE A SNAPSHOT IN DISK (user requirement 2026-06-12, hard). In addition to the periodic timer, a final btrfs checkpoint is written on the way down — every reboot and every shutdown, before filesystems unmount. Apps flush their session stores (browser tabs, editor state, KDE session) when the session ends, so this snapshot captures the freshest possible file-state of the session being closed.

reboot_with_session._comment: `sudo reboot-with-session` — the RAM-session counterpart for restarts: writes the FULL hibernate image to the swapfile, then REBOOTS (kernel disk-mode 'reboot') instead of powering off. At the rEFInd menu that follows: NixOS - Primary (default) resumes the saved session; NixOS - Fresh Desktop starts clean and discards it. Implemented via a runtime /run/systemd/sleep.conf.d drop-in (HibernateMode=reboot) that exists only for this invocation — /run is tmpfs, so a completed reboot wipes it and the battery-watchdog's critical hibernate keeps normal power-off semantics. Use plain Restart or Fresh Desktop when booting a NEW kernel is the point (resuming the image returns to the old one by design).

restore._comment: How to use a checkpoint. Single file: plain copy out of the snapshot path (read-only, browsable like a normal directory). Full home rollback: boot a rescue entry, `mv @home-diego @home-diego.broken && btrfs subvolume snapshot /mnt/btrfs-root/@snapshots/home-diego/<ts> /mnt/btrfs-root/@home-diego` (writable snapshot-of-snapshot), reboot.

testers._comment: Run via test-session-checkpoint.sh (same data-driven runner pattern as test-hibernation.sh).

checks.description: at least one checkpoint snapshot exists on disk
newest checkpoint is a read-only btrfs snapshot (immutable session file)
checks.command: btrfs property get "/mnt/btrfs-root/@snapshots/home-diego/$(ls -1 /mnt/btrfs-root/@snapshots/home-diego/ | sort | tail -1)" ro

checks.description: session-checkpoint-shutdown is wired into shutdown.target — every reboot/shutdown writes a final snapshot (full proof appears in the journal of the NEXT boot as a '-shutdown' suffixed checkpoint)
reboot-with-session command is installed (RAM-session snapshot + reboot)
checkpoint service runs idle IO class — can never trash the interactive session (systemd reports the class numerically: 3 = idle)
